# 2026-11-08

**Crow Control now shows the engineering roadmap's state, generated by script.** The founder console's new Worker went live at about 09:02 UTC. Its data passed the new Worker's check on the first build. Every fact below is measured unless it says otherwise.

The roadmap lives in the founders' private repository as one data file. A script writes the roadmap page and a small view file from it. The view holds only IDs, ranks, stages, approved short labels and status, and Crow Control reads only that view. Adding an item is one command.

## Waiting on Rafa

- **Check control.escrow.stream:** the "Roadmap ›" link in the header, and the Roadmap block with stages, in flight, next up, parked and private. The page sits behind GitHub sign-in, so the coordinator could not open it.

## Decided today

- **Crow Control reads a small publishable view of the roadmap, not the full file.** Rafa: "Switch to view file". The console build runs public holdback code beside `control/`, so the view carries no task text.
- **Adding a roadmap item is a light change.** Rafa: "adding one item should be a super light change and shouldn't cost 100k tokens to update the entire flow". One command adds the item, then a push and a page republish. There is no PR, review or agent for a data-only edit, and the tests check rules, never today's data.
- **The console build stays twice a day,** at 07:07 and 16:07 Berlin time, plus "Run workflow" (unchanged since 2026-11-05).

## Token cost

The roadmap pipeline ran well over its budgets, as reported by each agent:

| Change | Budget | Tokens | Tool calls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Step 1: the data and the script | 150,000 | 327,550 | 103 |
| Step 2: the console blocks | 60,000 | 221,930 | 84 |
| Step 2: the review fix | (same change) | 238,653 | 16 |
| The flow test's one-time fixes | 80,000 | 181,592 | 64 |

The first item added through the pipeline found two bugs, now fixed:
- the ID allocator counted test fixtures as IDs in use;
- 13 tests pinned the migration day's data.

The next item added with the one-command adder measures the steady-state cost.
